items.headline: OM Defence Systems runs X7 interceptor at TRL 5 through NATO TIE26 and BATT26; no contracts, TRL 6 targeted for early 2027
items.summary: UK-based OM Defence Systems is demonstrating its X7 one-way counter-drone interceptor to NATO and British Army users, aiming to replace the FPV pilot with an operator authorising engagements through the company's ground control station. Co-founder Oliver Anderson said "there is significant interest in the system we are demonstrating," and that the end state is "to remove the FPV pilot and let an operator control the engagement via our ground control station. That is what lets us scale the system to protect critical national infrastructure." The system sits at technology readiness level 5, with TRL 6 targeted in early 2027 and no contracts awarded. The X7 has three elements — interceptor, networked launch pad, ground control station — with the aircraft described as capable of over 400 km/h and designed against Group 1, 2 and 3 UAS. The ground control station accepts feeds from multiple radars and ingests sensor data using the SAPIENT communications standard, so targeting can come from any external sensor network rather than a dedicated radar. The X7 operated in full autonomous mode at TRL 5 in field demonstrations with the British Army in March 2026, and the ground control station was taken to NATO's Technical Interoperability Exercise TIE26 (May 11-22) and BATT26 in Latvia (Aug. 4-14). Alongside X7, the company fields Shadow, described as TRL 9 and in use with the Armed Forces of Ukraine, with 500 produced in 2025 and 1,500 planned for 2026; Anderson said Shadow went to PCC6 trials in California and will support the UK's 16 Air Assault Brigade on exercise in October.
items.why_it_matters: The only line worth extracting is the architectural one: engagement decisions and sensor fusion sit in a ground control station consuming SAPIENT feeds, not on the interceptor. That is the opposite of the on-platform bet — it is a nearby server the effector streams to, and it fails when the link to the launch pad fails. It is also a reminder that in Europe the interoperability standard, not the inference, is the integration point buyers ask about. No tracked customer or competitor is involved; file and move on.

items.headline: Army paid General Dynamics $533M for a Mesquite artillery plant that never produced a usable shell; GD has since taken $2.5B in new awards
items.summary: The Army funded a General Dynamics artillery shell factory in Mesquite, Texas, at a cost of $533 million, and according to a July Department of Defense inspector general report the facility never produced a single usable shell. Former workers described imported Turkish machinery failing repeatedly through 2024 — robot arms drenched in oil catching fire, one blaze melting a robot's cables for a week, steel blocks dropped five feet, and press machines requiring "a bunch of guys taking turns going at the machine with a sledgehammer every night," in the words of former employee Quantel White. The Army ordered work halted on two of the plant's three production lines in August 2025 after General Dynamics missed eight deadlines; the third line continued. The Army has not required repayment and General Dynamics remains in charge of the facility. Since the shutdown, General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems has received contract awards totalling $2.5 billion. Turkish subcontractor Repkon's American offshoot, renamed Paligen Technologies, received a no-bid $435 million Army contract to set up a TNT factory. The inspector general report named no companies or individuals and recommended the Army determine whether the contract was "appropriately issued" and how "the money was spent." One former Army official called it "an absolute disaster" and said "the Army should've gone after recovering money from General Dynamics."
items.why_it_matters: No sensor, C2 or autonomy content — this is munitions industrial base. The one transferable read is on acquisition mechanics: an award of this size failed for two years with no clawback, no named accountability in the IG report, and $2.5B in follow-on business to the same vendor. That is the environment any argument about speed-based acquisition reform has to survive, and it is ammunition for whoever on the Hill wants to re-impose contracting guardrails on the fast pathways this reader depends on to compete.
